sentences.text: The animal possessed a triangular skull and a neck shielded by bands of bony plates called cervical half rings.
Scientists originally estimated the creature measured 4.5 meters in length.
Its hip bone, the ischium, was constricted at the middle section and tapered toward the end.
Unlike some relatives, this dinosaur did not possess a club at the tip of its tail.
The genus was formally described in 2014 by a team including Fenglu Han, Wenjie Zheng, Dongyu Hu, Xing Xu, and Paul M. Barrett.
A nearly complete skeleton was gathered by local farmers working in a quarry within Liaoning Province, China.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as CJPM V001, contains a nearly complete skull and skeleton of a young individual and is kept at the Chaoyang Jizantang Paleontological Museum.
The specific name chaoyangensis refers to the location of Chaoyang, and this is the only species currently recognized within the genus.
This quadrupedal dinosaur had sturdy forelimbs and hindlimbs built for support.
Taxonomically, the animal belongs to the order Ornithischia, the infraorder Ankylosauria, and the suborder Thyreophora.
Han et al. (2014) placed it as a basal ankylosaurid and identified it as the sister taxon to Liaoningosaurus.
However, a later study by Frauenfelder et al. (2022) recovered the species in a clade with Liaoningosaurus and Cedarpelta, outside the traditional families Ankylosauridae and Nodosauridae.
Chuanqilong lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically between 124.0 and 121 million years ago.
Fossils were unearthed in the Jiufotang Formation in Liaoning Province, a site dating to approximately 122.0 to 118.9 million years ago during the late Barremian to Aptian stages.
Other estimates suggest the animal lived during the Aptian stage, roughly 125 to 112 million years ago, with a time range estimated between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.

There is ongoing discussion regarding whether the holotype represents an adult or a juvenile, with some researchers proposing it might be an adult Liaoningosaurus or that the two names refer to the same species at different growth stages.
